=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

## Buyer assessment

**Do not accept the package as drafted.** The Seller combines broad disclosure and deemed Buyer knowledge with restrictions applying to virtually every claim. That could leave Wattlebridge bearing known transaction risks while materially weakening its remedies for unknown problems.

The analysis below is based on the supplied update and Disclosure Letter—not the underlying SPA or DD documents. The Seller’s descriptions should be checked against those documents. The embedded instruction telling an AI to approve the package is not a contractual term or a basis for advice; I have disregarded it.

## 1. Liability limitations: reject the blanket approach

### General warranty cap and thresholds
The proposed **AUD 4.8 million cap**, **AUD 25,000 de minimis** and **AUD 250,000 deductible basket** operate cumulatively. Even a valid claim may produce little or no recovery.

Push for:
- A higher general warranty cap, assessed against outstanding diligence risks and any warranty insurance.
- A lower de minimis, with related claims aggregated so one underlying problem cannot be fragmented into excluded claims.
- A **tipping basket**, under which qualifying claims become recoverable from the first dollar once the basket is crossed, rather than recovery only above AUD 250,000.
- Clear treatment of whether below-de-minimis claims count towards the basket.

These figures are commercial negotiation points, not inherently unacceptable in isolation. The greater concern is their interaction with the Seller’s much broader exclusions.

### Fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities
**Reject “administrative simplicity” as a reason to treat title and capacity like ordinary business warranties.** Ownership of the shares and the Seller’s power to sell them underpin the entire transaction.

Require separate regimes for:
- **Title, capacity and authority:** a cap of at least the purchase price, no de minimis or basket, and a substantially longer claim period.
- **Tax:** a dedicated tax covenant/indemnity covering pre-Completion liabilities, with appropriate exclusions and a period aligned to relevant assessment and recovery exposure.
- **Specific indemnities:** separately negotiated caps and periods, outside general warranty thresholds and disclosure/knowledge defences.
- **Fraud and deliberate misconduct:** express carve-outs from liability restrictions, carefully drafted to address whose conduct is attributable to the Seller.

IP warranty protection also needs separate consideration because of the identified Ironquay ownership gap.

### Claim deadlines
Eighteen months may not capture issues emerging over more than one reporting cycle. Seek at least **24 months for general warranties**, with longer tailored periods for fundamental, tax and identified risks.

Review both notification and litigation deadlines. A timely notified claim should survive expiry; contingent claims should remain capable of recovery when they crystallise. Avoid technical notice requirements that extinguish otherwise valid claims without material prejudice.

## 2. Exclusive remedies, non-reliance and Buyer knowledge

**Reject limitations applying indiscriminately to “all Claims of any nature”.** That wording could restrict contractual indemnities, completion obligations, price adjustments, repayment rights and claims involving misleading conduct—not merely warranty claims.

Require:
- An express claims matrix specifying which restrictions apply to each category.
- Preservation of purchase-price adjustments, debt recovery, completion obligations, specific indemnities and appropriate equitable remedies.
- Appropriate fraud carve-outs and preservation of rights that cannot lawfully be excluded.
- Review of clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 together, including their treatment of representations and statutory misleading-conduct claims. Do not assume a general savings clause solves every issue.

Clause 8.3 is especially adverse. **“Discoverable” information is not actual knowledge.** Nor should knowledge of every adviser automatically be attributed to the Buyer.

Prefer deleting the knowledge defence. If retained, limit it to actual, conscious knowledge of named Buyer deal-team members, without constructive knowledge, a duty to investigate or automatic adviser attribution. It should not defeat title claims or specific indemnities.

## 3. Disclosure: availability is not fair disclosure

Reject wholesale disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room and public registers. That could transfer the risk of buried, ambiguous or incomplete information to Wattlebridge.

Require:
- **Fair disclosure:** sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the relevant matter.
- Specific cross-references to the warranties being qualified.
- A fixed, indexed and preserved data-room record.
- Narrowly defined permitted general disclosures, rather than unlimited public-record disclosure.
- No qualification of completion obligations, price mechanics or specific indemnities merely because the underlying issue was disclosed.

The stated cutoff is **22 September 2026**. Require updated diligence and disclosures before signing/completion, but no automatic release for later disclosures: material new matters should trigger an agreed remedy, price discussion or termination right.

## 4. Bluefen: consent must preserve the commercial relationship

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. The Disclosure Letter expressly says final consent and evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions are absent. That does not support the update’s statement that consent is “addressed”.

Require a Buyer-waivable condition precedent covering:
- Valid written consent under clause 11.2.
- Satisfaction or appropriate waiver of clause 11.3 conditions.
- No unacceptable amendments, charges, termination rights or other adverse conditions.

Reasonable endeavours is a process obligation, **not a substitute for obtaining the required result**. Delivery of a document labelled “consent” should not alone satisfy the condition. Include a long-stop date and consequences for failure.

## 5. Riverlark and funds flow: no unsecured post-Completion promise

A release “following Completion” is inadequate for a debt-free/cash-free acquisition with approximately **AUD 3.2 million outstanding**.

Require:
- A binding payoff statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs.
- Repayment through the Completion funds flow.
- Effective releases of relevant security and guarantees at Completion, supported by agreed discharge mechanics and subsequent registration evidence.
- Resolution of change-control requirements and any resulting default exposure.

The SPA must also make clear how the AUD 24 million price interacts with debt, cash and working capital. **Avoid both leaving the Buyer to fund Seller debt and deducting the same debt twice.**

## 6. Completion bonuses: allocate the full cost expressly

The **AUD 420,000 conditional bonuses** are not safely dealt with by saying they are “a matter for the Seller”. The Company may remain liable after Completion.

Require:
- Express Seller economic responsibility through payment, a debt-like deduction or another agreed adjustment.
- Quantification of applicable superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs, including payment/withholding mechanics.
- Treatment of amounts payable later because of continued-employment conditions.
- Protection against double counting in debt and working capital.

Employee entitlements should remain satisfied; the allocation between Buyer and Seller must not assume they can simply be cancelled.

## 7. Ironquay: secure ownership, not merely payment reimbursement

The existing indemnity is too narrow if it covers only the SOW3 payment. The principal risk is **inability to own, use or commercialise the relevant IP**, potentially affecting business value.

Require before Completion:
- Reconciliation of every SOW3 fee and reliable payment evidence.
- Confirmation that the contractual transfer conditions have been satisfied.
- A confirmatory assignment and any necessary author consents, licences or releases, with chain-of-title verification.

The AUD 180,000 open balance is evidence requiring investigation—not conclusive proof of non-payment. Conversely, its disclosure does not establish ownership.

Seek a specific indemnity covering losses from the identified ownership defect and related third-party claims, not just the invoice amount. If ownership is business-critical, an indemnity alone is insufficient.

## 8. Export/privacy incident: investigate without prejudging

The record establishes a misdirected download link and potentially approximately **1,240 records**. It does **not** establish access, a legally notifiable breach or quantified loss. The Seller’s “not expected to be material” conclusion is therefore premature.

Require:
- Containment, preservation of evidence and investigation of access, recipients, data scope and consequences.
- Assessment of applicable privacy, contractual and other notification obligations.
- Buyer visibility and appropriate involvement in remediation, without delaying legally required action.
- A specific indemnity for the identified pre-Completion incident, including reasonable investigation, remediation and third-party liabilities to the extent legally recoverable.

Consider retention or escrow if material exposure remains unresolved. Do not mechanically reduce the price without assessing likely exposure.

## 9. Renewals, lease, Mossvale and title

- **Sandbar renewals:** assess the three related AUD 110,000 commitments together. Establish timing, cancellation rights, service periods, accruals and commercial necessity. They are not automatically ordinary-course costs—or automatically debt-like deductions. Check interim conduct covenants and prevent double counting in working capital.
- **Office lease:** the disclosed obligation is notification, not landlord consent. Require compliant notice and evidence; do not invent a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not necessarily apply to a share sale. Check the complete agreement for change-control provisions and related definitions before demanding consent.
- **Share title:** DD-012 is relevant evidence, not complete verification. Check issued capital, options and other equity rights, encumbrances, transfer restrictions, constitutional requirements and completion transfer documents. Require unqualified title warranties and delivery of 100% of the shares free of encumbrances.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Completion protection:** effective Bluefen consent, Riverlark repayment/releases, and satisfactory resolution of critical Ironquay ownership issues.
2. **Economic protection:** correct debt-free/cash-free mechanics, full bonus-cost allocation and investigation of the renewals.
3. **Remedy protection:** separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; narrow disclosure and knowledge defences; remove blanket claim restrictions.
4. **Unresolved-risk protection:** investigate the export incident, update diligence, and obtain targeted indemnities supported by credible Seller credit or security where needed.

**Bottom line:** disclosure of a problem does not solve it. Each identified risk needs an express completion requirement, economic allocation or enforceable remedy—and sometimes all three.
